materials.title: Renting a flat
materials.instructions: You will hear a telephone conversation between a letting agent and a woman who is looking for a flat.
materials.audioScript:
AGENT: Good afternoon, Harbour Lettings, this is Ben speaking.
CALLER: Hello. I'm calling about the flat on Fenwick Street that's advertised on your website.
AGENT: Ah yes, the one-bedroom flat. Can I take your name?
CALLER: It's Sofia Lindqvist. That's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T.
AGENT: Thanks, Sofia. So, the rent is eight hundred and fifty pounds a month, and that includes water but not electricity or internet.
CALLER: OK. And how much is the deposit?
AGENT: It's equal to five weeks' rent, so just under a thousand pounds.
CALLER: Right. Is the flat furnished?
AGENT: Partly. There's a bed, a wardrobe and a sofa, and the kitchen has a fridge and a washing machine, but there's no dishwasher.
CALLER: That's fine. What floor is it on?
AGENT: The third floor, and I should say there's no lift, so it's stairs only.
CALLER: Hmm. And is there any parking?
AGENT: Not with the flat, I'm afraid, but there's a bus stop right outside, and the train station is about a ten-minute walk.
CALLER: Good. When would it be available?
AGENT: From the first of March. The current tenant moves out at the end of February.
CALLER: Could I see it this week?
AGENT: Let me check. I could do Thursday at half past five, or Saturday morning at ten.
CALLER: Saturday would be better.
AGENT: Fine. When you come, please bring some photo ID. And if you decide to apply, we'll need a reference from your employer.
CALLER: No problem. Thanks very much.

materials.title: Tour of a reopened library
materials.instructions: You will hear a guide describing the changes to a city library.
materials.audioScript:
GUIDE: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the newly reopened Central Library. After two years of building work, I'm delighted to show you what's changed. Let me start with a quick overview of the four floors.
GUIDE: Here on the ground floor you'll find the main desk, where you can join the library and collect reserved books. We've also moved the café down here; it used to be on the top floor, but people found it too hard to reach. The café is open until six, an hour after most of the building closes on weekdays.
GUIDE: The first floor is now the children's library. It has a reading garden on the balcony, which is a completely new feature, and story sessions take place there every Wednesday afternoon.
GUIDE: On the second floor you'll find the adult lending collection and the quiet study area. Please note that phone calls aren't allowed anywhere on this floor. There are forty study desks, and these can now be booked online up to a week in advance.
GUIDE: The third floor houses our local history archive. Visitors can look at old maps, newspapers and photographs, but you'll need to make an appointment with the archivist first, because many items are fragile.
GUIDE: A few other changes. Membership is still free, but printing now costs ten pence per page, and you pay using your library card rather than coins. We've also installed self-service machines for returning books, so you no longer need to queue at the desk.
GUIDE: Finally, we're looking for volunteers to help with our homework club for teenagers, which runs on Monday and Thursday evenings. If you're interested, please leave your details at the main desk.

materials.title: Field trip report on coastal erosion
materials.instructions: You will hear two geography students, Hana and Marcus, discussing their field trip report with their tutor.
materials.audioScript:
TUTOR: Come in, Hana, Marcus. How did the field trip to the coast go?
HANA: Really well, thanks. We managed to measure the cliff at all five survey points.
TUTOR: Good. And what did you find?
MARCUS: The biggest surprise was the rate of erosion at the northern end. We expected it to be the fastest at the southern end, because that's where the sea defences were removed, but actually the north has lost more.
TUTOR: Any idea why?
HANA: We think it's because of the type of rock. The north is mostly soft clay, whereas the south is sandstone, which is much harder.
TUTOR: That makes sense. How did you collect your data?
MARCUS: We used tape measures to record the distance from fixed fence posts to the cliff edge, and then compared it with measurements from five years ago.
TUTOR: Were there any problems?
HANA: One of the fence posts had disappeared completely, so for that point we had to use aerial photographs instead.
TUTOR: Right. You'll need to explain that in your methods section, because it affects the reliability of that figure.
MARCUS: OK. We weren't sure whether to include photos in the report.
TUTOR: Definitely include them, but put them in an appendix rather than the main text, otherwise the report will be too long.
HANA: And for the conclusion, we wanted to recommend rebuilding the sea wall in the north.
TUTOR: I'd be careful there. A sea wall can just move the erosion further along the coast. You might suggest it as one option, but compare it with others, such as planting vegetation on the cliff.
MARCUS: That's a good idea. When's the deadline again?
TUTOR: The end of next week, Friday. And please submit it online, not on paper.

materials.title: Lecture: how migrating birds navigate
materials.instructions: You will hear part of a lecture about bird navigation.
materials.audioScript:
LECTURER: Today we're going to look at one of the great puzzles of biology: how migrating birds find their way. Some species fly thousands of kilometres each year and return to exactly the same nesting site, so they clearly have remarkable navigation skills.
LECTURER: Researchers believe birds use several different methods. The first is the sun. Experiments in the 1950s showed that birds kept in cages became restless and faced the correct direction for migration when they could see the sun, but became confused when the sky was hidden. To use the sun accurately, of course, a bird must also allow for the time of day, which means it needs an internal clock.
LECTURER: Many birds migrate at night, however, and these species appear to use the stars. In a famous series of experiments, young birds were raised in a planetarium, a building where an artificial night sky can be projected onto a ceiling. The birds learned to orient themselves around the point in the sky that appeared to rotate least, which in nature would be close to the Pole Star.
LECTURER: A third method involves the Earth's magnetic field. It's now thought that some birds can actually sense magnetic fields, possibly through special proteins in their eyes. Interestingly, this magnetic sense seems to be disturbed by certain kinds of electronic noise, which may be a growing problem in cities.
LECTURER: Finally, as birds get closer to their destination, they rely more on landmarks such as coastlines, rivers and mountains. Some seabirds may even use smell to locate their home island.
LECTURER: Understanding these systems is not just of scientific interest. Light pollution from buildings can attract night-migrating birds and cause many of them to die in collisions, so some cities now encourage office buildings to switch off their lights during peak migration periods.
